newsitem.title: FRANCE: Separate talks for Jerusalem holy sites -Charette.
newsitem.headline: Separate talks for Jerusalem holy sites -Charette.

text.p: French Foreign Minister Herve de Charette was quoted on Tuesday as saying that negotiations between Israel and the Palestinians about Jerusalem should be accompanied by separate international talks on its holy sites.

"The (permanent) status of Jerusalem will be agreed in the framework of talks between Israelis and Palestinians. But there are also religious aspects which are the concern of the three religions (Islam, Christianity and Judaism)," de Charette told the French Jewish weekly Tribune Juive.

"That is a separate question from the city's status. And it will be up to the three religions to establish a status for the holy sites. When a status is established for the city and another for the holy sites, the solution will have been found for Jerusalem," he said.
Asked whether he meant the status of the holy sites should be subject to international negotiations, de Charette replied: "Yes, that is it."

Israeli-Palestinian accords signed in Washington in 1993 call for permanent settlement talks between this year about Jerusalem but make no mention of separate discussions among religious authorities about the city's holy sites.
The Vatican has long said it wished to be consulted on the issue and both the Saudi and Jordanian monarchies have indicated similar desires over the past years.

The last legal basis for such an international role is thought to have been the ill-fated 1947 United Nations partition plan for Palestine, which suggested Jerusalem be a "separate body" with each religion administering its holy sites.
France, although a secular state, indicated at the time it wanted to be among administrators of Christian sites.
The French, Spanish and Belgian consuls-general in Jerusalem are regarded by the Roman Catholic authorities as representatives of "protecting powers".
